- Model consistently underestimates prices in early periods of the 30-day forecast horizon, especially after recent spikes.
- Overestimates prices in the first 5–10 days of the forecast, then gradually converges toward true values — suggesting a lag in adjusting to recent trends.
- After sharp price spikes, model overshoots in the immediate aftermath (e.g., +5–10% above true value) and then corrects, indicating a failure to fully capture mean reversion.
- Model exhibits persistent downward bias in later forecast days (e.g., 25–30), particularly when true values are rising or stabilizing.
- When true values show strong downward momentum, model fails to recognize it and continues to forecast higher prices — suggesting underweighting of negative trend signals.
- Model tends to overreact to short-term volatility, especially in the first 5–7 days, leading to overcorrection or overshoot.
- In periods of low volatility or consolidation, model underestimates the true value, often by 1–3% — suggesting it underweights the “mean” or “baseline” price.
- Model does not adjust for seasonality or calendar effects (e.g., end-of-month or quarterly adjustments) — leading to persistent bias in certain windows.
- When true values are near or below historical mean, model continues to forecast higher — indicating failure to recognize mean reversion or “reversion to baseline” behavior.
- Model tends to overestimate prices in the final 5–7 days of the forecast, especially when true values are trending downward — suggesting a “tail risk” or “end-of-horizon” bias.
